name: Marce Choke
description: Master the Marce Choke in BJJ - a powerful gi-specific lapel choke from top positions. Complete setup, execution, defense, and safety protocols for competition.
target_area: Carotid arteries and trachea via lapel compression
variant_uniqueness: Lapel-as-ligature creates noose effect from top control
summary: The Marce Choke is a gi-specific lapel strangle applied from dominant top positions such as side control and north-south, using the opponent's own lapel as a ligature around the neck to compress both carotid arteries.
overview:
The Marce Choke is a highly effective gi-specific submission that combines elements of the loop choke and cross collar choke mechanics. This technique leverages the opponent's own lapel to create a powerful blood choke from dominant top positions, particularly side control and north-south. The Marce Choke is particularly effective because it uses the mechanical advantage of the lapel wrapped around the opponent's neck, creating compression on both carotid arteries simultaneously while controlling the opponent's upper body.

Unlike traditional collar chokes that require both hands on the lapel, the Marce Choke uses one hand on the lapel and your body weight to apply pressure, making it extremely difficult to defend once properly set. The technique excels in gi competition because it can be applied from multiple top positions and often catches opponents by surprise as they focus on defending more common submissions.

The choke works on a fundamental principle: using the lapel as a ligature around the neck while your body weight and positioning create the constricting force. This makes it a high-percentage technique for practitioners who master the proper setup and understand the mechanics of lapel manipulation. The finishing mechanic relies on opposing forces - the lapel pulls from one direction while chest pressure drives from the other - creating a noose effect that is biomechanically efficient and extremely difficult to defend through strength alone.

injury_risks.injury: Carotid artery compression leading to unconsciousness
injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate recovery if released promptly; potential for injury if held too long
Minutes to hours of discomfort; days if excessive force applied

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum in training, allowing clear tap opportunity
tap_signals: Physical hand tap on opponent or mat
release_protocol: Immediately release lapel grip upon tap signal
Remove body weight from opponent's torso
Unwrap lapel from around neck if entangled
Allow partner time to recover before continuing training
training_restrictions: Never apply full pressure in initial learning phases
Never hold the choke after tap or loss of consciousness
Always ensure training partner can tap with at least one hand
Never use competition speed or intensity in drilling
Stop immediately if partner shows any signs of distress beyond normal discomfort

variations_and_setups.description: From north-south position, feed the far lapel across their neck and drive your chest straight down into their face while maintaining the lapel grip. This variation often provides better leverage and makes it harder for the opponent to turn into you.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent is defending well from side control or when you naturally transition to north-south during scrambles. Particularly effective against opponents who are good at recovering guard from side control.

variations_and_setups.variation_name: Marce Choke from Knee on Belly
variations_and_setups.description: Establish knee on belly position, then reach across to grip the far lapel. Feed it across their neck, then transition your knee to the mat and drive your chest down to finish. The knee on belly provides excellent control during the setup phase.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: Against opponents who react strongly to side control pressure by trying to turn in. Knee on belly gives you more mobility to follow their movement while setting up the choke.

variations_and_setups.description: From kesa gatame (scarf hold), reach across with your far hand to grip their far lapel, feed it across their neck, then use your near-side arm to control their head while your body weight drives the choke. Your head positioning is crucial - it should be low and tight to their head.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When you have a strong scarf hold position established. This variation is particularly effective in gi competition as it combines positional control with submission threat.
